unplaced.en: "The one who proceeds." Because for the Greeks the word logos has so wide a range and is a homonym, Maximus rightly distinguished it from the logos that is uttered by the mouth. For the inward logos (logos endiathetos), the speech of the mind and of the heart, lodged within it, of which he speaks at such length in the preface of the Scholia to the Questions to Thalassius, is rather the parent of action and holds whatever of goodness is in it. On this matter see Gregory's oration on the great Athanasius.

unplaced.text: Τῆς μὲν ὀδύνης, ἡ ἡδονή. Sunt quidem hæc, alia aliis causa, uti aliis locis ipse Maximus explicat; dumque sectamur voluptatem, nos laboribus implicamus, ac dolorem augemus, ipsumque jugem reddimus. Hic tamen, et quod attinet ad rationem Maximo allatam, potius scribendum videatur, τῆς μὲν ἡδονῆς, ἡ ὀδύνη· Dolor causa est voluptatis; quod ejus depellendi causa, voluptatem consectamur. unplaced.anchorLine: νης, ἡ ἡδονή (b)· θέλοντες γὰρ ἐκφυγεῖν τὴν κατὰ
unplaced.en: "Of pain, pleasure." These things are so indeed, one being the cause of another, as Maximus himself explains elsewhere; and while we pursue pleasure we entangle ourselves in toils, increase pain, and make it lasting. Yet here, in view of the reasoning Maximus gives, one should rather write "of pleasure, pain": pain is the cause of pleasure, since we pursue pleasure in order to drive pain away. Perhaps Maximus wrote it more fully; although it is easy to see these words exchanged because of the likeness of their letters.

Videtur τὴν ἔμπρακτον ζωήν, quasi activam dicere, seu, quæ actionem colit, et contra Θεωρητικὴν dividitur : velitque plures non admodum exercitatos in vita activa et actionis cultu, quasi per rationes superiores vi contemplationis Deoque illustrante prudentiæ munere nactos esse. Anceps usus τοῦ, κατὰ, dubium sensum reddit. Verius hic Maximus dixerit, quam in cap. De cha[...]itate ad Elpidium, esse aliqua difficilia, et quæ semel et iterum legi oporteat, ut percipiantur, nec solum ex phrasi et usu loquendi, sed magis ex ipsa materia, ipsa ex reconditiore penu moralis et Christianæ philosophiæ petita.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἐμπράκτου ζωῆς (d), καὶ τὸ φρονεῖν ἐκληρώσαντο.
unplaced.en: "By the lack of the active life." He seems to mean by "the active life" (so to speak the practical life), the one that cultivates action and is divided off against the contemplative; and he wishes that many, not greatly practised in the active life and the cultivation of action, had obtained the gift of prudence as it were through higher reasons, by the power of contemplation and with God shedding light. The ambiguous use of "κατά" leaves the sense doubtful. Maximus might more truly say here, as in the chapter On Charity to Elpidius, that there are some difficult matters which must be read once and again to be understood, not only from the phrasing and the way of speaking, but still more from the subject matter itself, drawn from the deeper store of moral and Christian philosophy.

Jungit Marcus semel et iterum, De just. et operibus, c. 122 et 133, τὸ, ἡδυπαθὴς et ἀνάλγητος, qui sit voluptarius, sicque corporis deliciis deditus, ut illis sensum omnem pietatis exuerit; nedum erga proximos, per immisericordiam, uti expressit Obsop., sed magis erga Deum propriamque salutem.
unplaced.anchorLine: μείῳ (e) μὴ αἰσχυνόμενος.
unplaced.en: "In the hospital of insensibility." Insensibility (analgesia) here in Maximus is plainly a stupor of mind by which a man lacks all sense of heavenly things and of what pertains to salvation, and can hardly, or not even hardly, be renewed to better fruit. Mark (the Hermit) joins together, again and again, in On Those Justified by Works, chapters 122 and 133, the words "given to pleasure" and "insensible": one who is a voluptuary and so given over to bodily delights that he has lost all sense of piety; much less toward neighbours, through lack of compassion, as Obsopoeus rendered it, but still more toward God and his own salvation.

unplaced.anchorLine: λε΄. Ὁ τῷ λυπήσαντι ἀδίκως (f) πρὸ τοῦ προσ-
unplaced.en: "He who has grieved (another) unjustly." I was compelled to alter what appeared wholly faulty and could not have been written by Maximus with any fitting sense, reading "having grieved justly, and repenting"; although otherwise the sense of the whole chapter is straightforward, pointed, and sets out learnedly the degrees of bearing or remitting injuries, which are injuries when they are inflicted unjustly. Instead of "repenting" I would have written "being well-disposed (metheunoon)", if I had found an approved author using that word. As it is, the word "eunoon" (well-disposed) is not unfitting, and Maximus may have had in view that saying in Matt. v, 25: "Be well-disposed toward your adversary quickly" ("Habeto benevolentiam cum adversario tuo cito", as Erasmus renders it, and as the Greek sounds); and this too looks to the reconciliation we seek, forgetting injuries, if anything of benevolence has been hurt, to repair it by a sounder counsel.

unplaced.en: "To bring forth anger from the heart." Among so many meanings of the verb paragō, which the Seventy used in that passage of Ecclesiastes [continued on p-0720]. [the Seventy] in that passage of Ecclesiastes, a sense not much attested among Greek authors. Yet it is akin to what is cited in the larger Lexicon of several authors (otherwise Crispin's), from Plutarch in the Life of Romulus: "Tatius was expelling these and sending them away", that is, he struck them out and dismissed them; which the Hebrew word also means, "he caused to pass over". In Paul, the phrase "for the fashion of this world passes away" (I Cor. vii, 31), which the Vulgate renders "the figure of this world passes", could equally be rendered "deceptive is the appearance of this world", because it presents itself to mortal eyes in human affairs; Paul calls his disciples' minds away from these, so that they do not let themselves be fooled by them by clinging to them, but carry all their zeal over to what truly is, the use of things being permitted only lightly and only so far as the necessity of life demands for those hastening elsewhere. For the Vulgate's "malitia" in place of "epithymias" (desire), from the Hebrew: the explanation of that word is "epithymia"; for this is the malice or vice of the flesh, concupiscence.

Nempe diuturniora gulæ prælia, nec nisi morte finienda; quod absolvi a necessario ciborum usu, quandiu vita superstes est, minime liceat; cui conjuncta illa gulæ voluptas, ipsa necessaria Deoque auctore insita, quandiu justæ mediocritatis modum servat. Secus de venereorum voluptate, ordinata ad speciei conservationem, cujus rei munus, nec ad omnes, nec pro omni statu aut ætate spectat. unplaced.en: "And the throat remains." That is, the battles of the gullet are the longer-lasting and can be ended only by death; for release from the necessary use of food is by no means allowed while life remains, and joined to it is the gullet's pleasure, itself necessary and planted by God, so long as it keeps the measure of due moderation. It is otherwise with the pleasure of sexual things, which is ordered to the preservation of the species, a function that does not concern all persons, nor every state or age. The text read in error "the throat having been relaxed" (pareimenou tou pharyngos); an error so evident, that of an unskilled scribe, I would not care to gloss over, nor could I, and so give the reader trouble.

Carnalis affectus, maxime venereorum, qui Maximo passim, ἐμπαθὴς λογισμός, ac jactu maxime consummatur; vere κατ' ἐξοχὴν πάθος, ob tactus majorem delectationem. ἡδυπάθεια, in aliis sensibus captata voluptas et jucunditas : προσπάθεια, mentis ipsa affectio, quæ se proclive abduci sinat. Sed hæc satis arbitraria, ut quæ sequentibus in his vocibus Græca facilitate Maximus ludit; quarum lepos atque vis, nullis satis Latinis vocibus potest repræsentari.

unplaced.en: "Empatheia." Carnal affection, above all of sexual things, which in Maximus is everywhere the "passionate thought"; and it is brought to completion above all by touch [printed 'jactu', the first letter damaged]; truly the passion par excellence, because of the greater delight of touch. Hedypatheia is pleasure and enjoyment taken in the other senses; prospatheia is the very inclination of the mind, which lets itself be readily led away. But these are rather arbitrary, as Maximus plays in the following chapters with these words in Greek with ease; their charm and force cannot be rendered by any Latin words.

unplaced.text: Ὑπομένειν ἡμᾶς τῇ πίστει. Sic legisse Maximum Rom. xii, 12, ubi nunc Græca, τῇ θλίψει, Vulg. in tribulatione patientes; nihil dubium : utque alii codices suffragarentur, illa lectio magis arrideret, quod præsertim constructio ipsa mollior; quodque adeo duplicem virtutem Paulus continua serie videtur commendare, ac cuique quod illi proprium aut conjunctum est, tribuere : spei, gaudium, τῇ ἐλπίδι χαίροντες· fidei, laborum sustinentiam, τῇ πίστει ὑπομένοντες· quod ipsum argumentum late prosequitur in Epist. ad Hebr., ostendens omni retro ævo sanctos illa victores laborum exstitisse : cum illud, τῇ θλίψει ὑπομένοντες, duram omnino constructionem habeat, et in qua aliquid desideretur, necessario supplendum; nec satis antecedentibus aut sequentibus cohæreat : tametsi habent etiam Chrys., Theodor., Theophyl., etc. Cumque superioribus illud hæserit, τῷ καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, quod repræsentant Græcæ omnes editiones (si forte Parisiensem τῶν LXX, seu illis adjunctam Novi Testam. ad exemplar Romanum expressam exceperis) Erasm. temporì servientes, sic abhorrente sententia, nec satis Paulo digna, pro eo quod legerunt antiqui omnes relati, et Vulg. habetque cod. Alexand. τῷ Κυρίῳ δουλεύοντες, Domino servientes; quid mirum potuisse, pro, τῇ πίστει, τῇ θλίψει, sic una serie textu ibi laborante obrepere? Maximo, ex meliori codice emendante; si tamen ille ex codice scripsit, non ut suggerebat memoria : quæ sæpius id repræsentat, non quod in codice legimus, sed quod κατὰ πρόχειρον accommodatius nobis videtur : quomodo etiam Hieronymo sæpius obrepsisse observat Joan. Morinus, in Exercit. biblicis; potiorique ratione aliis, quorum in divinis non tanta fuit ἀκρίβεια. Hincque est, ut nihil affirmare ausim, ac donec occurrant certiora monumenta, mutandum contendere. Satis fuit aliam ejus loci lectionem, quæ tanti videatur, Maximo auctore utcunque vindicare ac declarare.
unplaced.anchorLine: πϛ΄. Ὑπομένειν μὲν ἡμᾶς τῇ πίστει (n) παρα-
unplaced.en: "That we endure by faith." Maximus read thus at Rom. xii, 12, where the Greek now has "in tribulation" (te thlipsei), the Vulgate "patient in tribulation"; no doubt of it: and even if other codices supported it, that reading would please more, since above all the construction itself is smoother, and Paul seems to commend a double virtue in continuous sequence, assigning to each what is proper or joined to it: to hope, joy ("rejoicing in hope"); to faith, endurance of labours ("enduring by faith"). Paul pursues this very argument at length in the Epistle to the Hebrews, showing that in every past age the saints were victors over labours. Whereas "enduring in tribulation" has a wholly harsh construction, one in which something must be supplied, and it does not cohere well with what precedes and follows, although Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, etc. have it. And since "serving the time" (to kairo douleuontes) has clung to the preceding words, which all Greek editions present (unless you except, perhaps, the Paris edition of the Septuagint, or the New Testament appended to it and printed after the Roman exemplar), Erasmus's "temporì servientes" is so at odds with the sense, and scarcely worthy of Paul, whereas all the ancients reported, and the Vulgate, and the Alexandrian codex have "serving the Lord" (to Kyrio douleuontes): what wonder that in place of "by faith" and "in tribulation" such a reading should creep in in a single sequence where the text is troubled? Maximus, correcting from a better codex, if indeed he wrote from a codex and not as memory suggested, which often reproduces not what we read in the codex but what comes more readily to hand: as Jean Morin observes in his Biblical Exercitations that it often happened to Jerome too, and with more reason to others, whose accuracy in divine matters was not so great. So I would dare assert nothing, and contend for a change only when more certain evidence turns up. It was enough to defend and set out, on Maximus's authority, another reading of that place that seems worth the notice.

Describit Marc. De justitia ex oper. c. 68, durum mentis certamen, cum ab occupata olim informatione, ἀπὸ χρονίας προλήψεως; avellendus est animus, quasi tortoribus hinc inde cor distrahentibus : ubi frigide Obsop. temporali occupatione.

unplaced.en: "In which he lingers." The thought is one he seems to have borrowed from an earlier author; it signifies that things done, and from custom, please, even if they are otherwise unpleasant. Mark (the Hermit), On Those Justified by Works, ch. 68, describes the hard struggle of the mind when it must be torn away from a long-held preoccupation (apo chronias propleipseos), as though torturers were pulling the heart apart on both sides; where Obsopoeus, flatly, has "temporali occupatione".

Iterum, c. 102, ὁ μονολόγιστον ἐξανύων εὐχήν, intra velamen versari Maximo dicitur, opponitque τῷ ἐν αὐτῇ ῥεμβομένῳ, qui vaga mente in ea sit, segniusque oret, nec sobria ac attenta mente. Nam et Chrysost. in Epist. ad Coloss. τῷ γρηγοροῦντι καὶ νήφοντι opponit : cui proinde idem est ac ἀκηδιῶν qui segnis tepidusque est : quo fere sensu etiam μετέωρον haud raro Patres dicunt : quod et Hesych. κοῦφον reddit et ἐνυπνιῶδες levem, stultum; suspensi scilicet vagique ac instabilis animi.

unplaced.en: "Prayer of a single thought (monologistos)." Hesychius explains it as "monoklonos", and Varinus after him: so the obscure is explained by the more obscure. Mark, On Those Justified by Works, ch. 140, has "monologiston hope", which he also says is obtained by renunciation. "When the mind prevails by denial the monologistos hope": where, the first time, it should be emended from Maximus to "by apoarnesis" (renunciation), for that word is not used in that sense in the simple form; apoarnesis is the giving up of things, and our own self-denial by which hope is thus made monologistos, and monologistos itself is obtained by grace; a word Hesychius explained as [...], as many faults have crept into his Lexicon. It fits very well that hope should be called monologistos, as being by no means divided in thoughts but of one undisturbed reasoning; and so with prayer. Not as Obsopoeus rendered it in Mark's passage, 'hope to be uniquely considered.' Again, ch. 102: the one who completes a monologistos prayer is said by Maximus to be within the veil, and he opposes him to the one tossed about (rhembomenos) in it, who with wandering mind is in it and prays rather listlessly, not with a sober and attentive mind. Chrysostom too, on Colossians, opposes it to the one who is watchful and sober, for whom, accordingly, it is the same as 'sluggish', i.e. one who is slack and lukewarm; in nearly which sense the Fathers also often say 'suspended' (meteoron), which Hesychius also renders 'light' and 'dreamy, light, foolish': that is, of a suspended, wandering and unstable mind.

Sive enim ipsam rei quidditatem intelligat, quod vocat νόημα (id est conceptum mentis ac intellectum), sive circa accidentia et proprietates discurrat, quod λογισμὸν indigetat, omnino necesse est, ut phantasma, quasi omnis ejus cognitionis basim, speculetur, in quo et accidentia, et ipsa essentia illis involuta, eluceat. Quintilianus, l. iii, c. 5 : Illud jam omnes fatentur, esse quæstiones aut in scripto, aut in non scripto : in scripto, sunt de jure : in non scripto, de re : illud legale, hoc rationale. Hermagoras atque eum secuti vocant, νομικὸν et λογικόν. Item Cicero, Tusc. l. iv : Habes ea quæ de perturbationibus enucleatius disputant Stoici : quæ λογικὰ appellant, quia asseruntur subtilius. Sic itaque hic Maximus, λογικά, non ipsa ratione prædita, sed quæ sic ratione percipiuntur ; et quæ rationalia, eadem cum Græcis vocis ὁμωνυμίᾳ cogimur dicere, quod non distinctæ voces, ut sunt τὸ νοητὸν et τὸ νοερὸν etsi nec in illis auctores satis accurati sunt, nec, raro eorum significata confundant, ac quod passive sonat, active accipiant, vicissimque.

unplaced.en: "But having come to be in sense-perception." These things are, as it were, enigmatic. What it is for the mind to be in sense-perception, and while it is in it to have conceptions and reasonings, that is, to understand things simply and with discursive thought, I scarcely grasp, unless Maximus means this, that the one who understands is never released, for this ... [the note breaks off at the foot of the page and continues on p-0726]. [...] by the act, by the imagination, which he ascribes to sense-perception. For whether the mind understands the very essence of a thing, which he calls noema (that is, a concept or understanding of the mind), or ranges over accidents and properties, which needs reasoning (logismos), it is altogether necessary that it contemplate the phantasm, as the basis of all its knowledge, in which both the accidents and the essence itself, wrapped up in them, shine forth. His "ta logika", meaning things understood by discursive reasoning (the word being used passively), is a little unusual. It is akin, however, to what the rhetoricians call the "logical status", the rational issue. Quintilian, III, 5: "All admit that questions are either in what is written or in what is not written: in what is written, they concern law; in what is not written, the matter: the former legal, the latter rational." Hermagoras and his followers call them nomikon and logikon. Likewise Cicero, Tusc. IV: "You have what the Stoics argue more minutely about the passions: which they call logika, because they are asserted more subtly." So here Maximus's logika are not things endowed with reason but things perceived by reason; and what are rational (rationalia) we are forced to call by the same word, by the Greeks' homonymy, because the words are not distinct, as are to noeton and to noeron, although the authors are not careful enough even there, and often confuse their meanings and take actively what sounds passive, and the reverse.

unplaced.en: Metaphrena: some call these metaxenia (sic). Suidas: the place between the shoulders, i.e. the region between the shoulders: the back, the dorsum. Portus adds: what lies behind the midriff; and he took it from the Vatican codex, whose words are: 'Metaphrena: the back, because it lies behind the phrenes; the phrenes are membranes between the heart and the liver.' That is, the parts situated behind the phrenes: for the phrenes are membranes between heart and liver. As for 'in the greenness (chlorotes) of gold,' which the Sixtine translator preferred to render, following Hilary and Augustine, 'in the viridity of gold,' rather than the Vulgate's rendering, the editor does not approve. For it is clear that verdure and greenness are not aptly said of gold (whatever Hilary may think, that some eternal vigor is signified by that word), but rather its yellow and pallor, which is the best colour of gold: for Galen is the authority that chloron is taken for ochron (pale); nor does Hippocrates use it otherwise. Pliny too understood it so in Dioscorides, book iii, ch. 79, on Smyrnium: 'having a bark black outside, chloron or whitish within'; he himself renders it, book xxvii, ch. 13: 'Its bark is black outside, pale inside.' When writers mean to signify a deep green they usually say leek-green (prasoeides), and 'as if leek-like'; it suits certain stones and herbs, never gold.

unplaced.text: Ὁ Ἀμορῥαῖος. Sic nimirum Deut. i, 44, cum xiv, 45, non Amorrhæus, sed Amalec et Chananæus dicantur, sic de monte exsilientes, in quo erant in insidiis (ἐγκαθήμενοι) eos conscidisse ac persecutos esse, qui vim fecerant ut transirent: quod scilicet Deo irato rem aggrediebantur, Moyse etiam dissuadente. Ὁ οἰκῶν, quod scribit, qui habitabat, cum Hebr. ac reliquis convenit; potuitque sic haberi in Græcis, quorum illi copia fuit, sive erant τῶν LXX, sive ἡ κοινή. Quod est cap. 175, οὐχὶ πλῆθος τῶν κακῶν, nullus decoquere possim, ut ita scripsisse putem Maximum, aut forte habuisse cod. Vatic., nisi forte κακῶν, ἀντὶ τοῦ, πόνων positum sit. Sed præstaret καλῶν· honesti quippe nomine virtutis labores potius veniant, quam mali; iique uni quasi exercitus intelligantur, qui terrendo dæmones sint, nec vero terreant, nisi adsit, quam Maximus exigit virium animi una conspiratio et consensus.
unplaced.anchorLine: ροδʹ. Πάλαι μὲν ὁ Ἀμοῤῥαῖος (e′) ἐν τῷ ὄρει οἰ-
unplaced.en: 'The Amorite.' Thus, indeed, in Deut. i, 44, compared with Num. xiv, 45, it is not the Amorite but Amalek and the Canaanite who are said to have rushed down from the mountain, so that those lying in ambush on it (enkathemenoi) cut them down and pursued them, who had made an attempt to cross over, namely because they were undertaking the matter with God angry and Moses even dissuading them. The 'ho oikon' (the one dwelling), which he writes as 'who dwelt,' agrees with the Hebrew and the rest; and it could so have been read in the Greek copies, of which he had a supply, whether they were those of the Seventy or the common text. As in chapter 175, 'not a multitude of evils', which I cannot digest, so that I suppose Maximus wrote it so, or perhaps the Vatican codex had it, unless perhaps 'kakon' (of evils) is set for 'of toils (ponon)'. But 'kalon' (of good things) would be better: for the name of virtue would rather have toils be honorable than evil; and these alone are to be understood as an army, which would be terrifying the demons, and yet not terrify, unless there were present what Maximus requires: the single conspiracy and consensus of the soul's powers.

unplaced.text: Ὑπὸ θηρὸς ὡς ὁ δηχθείς. Quin scriptum sit Maximo, ὑπὸ θηρὸς ὄφεως, nullus dubito. unplaced.anchorLine: πηγάς, ὑπὸ [ὄφεως] θηρὸς ὡς ὁ δηχθείς (f)· ψυχὴ
unplaced.en: 'By a beast, like one bitten.' I have no doubt that Maximus wrote 'by a beast of a serpent.' unplaced.text: Ποῦ κοιτάζεις ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ τοὺς ἄρνας σου. Expressum ex Heb. [Hebrew word, not transcribed], quod est hiphil, ac proinde activam habet significationem, seu transitivam: quam potuit non mutare Syxt. interp. ea ipse religione, qua servaverant oἱ LXX. Idem peccat Gent. Hervetus in Greg. Nyssen. ad eum versum, ubi perinde reddit, ubi cubes; cum auctore Gregorio Sponsa sibi locum ostendi petat, in quo ipse Pastor bonus oves pascat, et accubare faciat. Eusebius quoque: Ἐὰν ἐν ταύτῃ με ποιμαίνῃς, κοιτάσῃς με πάντως ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ· Si me in salutari hac pascua paveris, prorsus in meridie collocabis: ἀντὶ τοῦ, Ἀναπαύσῃς ἐν τῷ ἀσκίῳ φωτὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως. Pro eo ac dicet Reficies, facies quiescere in loco resurrectionis, ubi nulla umbra est. Denique extra exemplum est, τὸ κοιτάζειν, ipsum esse τὸ, κοιτάζεσθαι, vel vocem cubare, aliam quam neutram ac intransitivam significationem habere. Hesych. κοιτάσαι, κατακοιμῆσαι· quod ipsum est, cubare facio, in lecto colloco; uti exponit Budæus: et ut alii metaphorice, sopio: suntque qui velint τὸ, κοιμῆσαι, pro κοιμίσαι scribi Æolice mutato ι in η. Est vero κομίσει eidem Hesych. κατακλίνει· quæ forma expressius activa est; etsi sunt alterius innumera exempla, ipsa pervia; haud forte satis illis animadversa, qui sic eam vocem quasi neutrali sensu, illique compositam τὸ, κοιτάσαι, acceperunt. Quæ sequitur vox in Maximo πεπλανημένη, errabunda, vagans, quomodo etiam habent Vulg. et versio Æthiopica, ipsa ex Græcis τῶν LXX expressa, in quibus interpres cum Maximo et ipse πεπλανημένη legerit; ni magis ut in Psello, illa vox expositio est ejus, quam ille habet, Maximus retinuit: Μήποτε γένωμαι ὡς παραβαλλομένη, πλανωμένη ἐπ᾽ ἀγέλης ἑτέρων σου· Ne fiam quasi decepta, vagabunda, errans, per occasionem gregis aliorum. Voxque Hebraica [Hebrew word, not transcribed] sic etiam exponitur; et non solum operuit, induit; quæ significatio haud satis huic loco congruit. Bene autem quam ex Psello, aliisque dixi. De Sponsa sermo est, sic sollicita inveniendi gregis Sponsi, et timentis in eo, per aliorum similitudinem, decipi, παραβαλεῖ· Hesych. ἀπατήσεις· decipies; hancque ejus vocis primam significationem ponit, ut notissimam et tritam. Suid. quoque, παραβλήδην, ἀπατητικῶς, παραλογιστικῶς. Nihilque ejus in eo occurrit ex Theucyd. quod Thesauri auctor studet elevare.
unplaced.anchorLine: σημβρίᾳ τοὺς ἄρνας σου (f)· ἵνα τούτοις ἀκολου-
unplaced.en: 'Where do you make your flock lie down at noon.' It is expressed from the Hebrew [Hebrew word], which is a hiphil and therefore has an active, that is transitive, signification; the Sixtine translator could have not changed it, with the same scruple with which the Seventy kept it. Gentian Hervet errs likewise in Gregory of Nyssa at that verse, where he renders it equally 'where you lie' (ubi cubes); whereas, on Gregory's authority, the Bride asks to be shown a place where the Good Shepherd himself pastures his sheep and makes them lie down. Eusebius also: 'If you shepherd me in this pasture, you will surely make me lie down at noon: that is, you will give me rest in the shadowless light of the resurrection'; in place of which he will say 'You will refresh, you will make rest in the place of the resurrection, where there is no shade.' Finally, it is unparalleled that koitazein should be the same as koitazesthai, or that the word 'to lie' should have a meaning other than neuter and intransitive. Hesychius: 'koitasai, katakoimesai,' which is, 'I make lie down, I put in a bed,' as Budaeus explains, and, as others, metaphorically, 'I put to sleep'; and there are those who would have koimesai written for koimisai with Aeolic change of iota to eta. And to the same Hesychius 'komisei' is 'kataklinei' (he lays down), a form more expressly active; though there are of the other usage innumerable examples, themselves open, not perhaps sufficiently noticed by those who took this word as if in neuter sense and compounded with it koitasai. The word that follows in Maximus, pepelanemene, 'wandering, straying', as the Vulgate and the Ethiopic version, itself drawn from the Seventy, have it, in which the translator along with Maximus himself read pepelanemene; unless rather, as in Psellus, that word is the explanation of the Hebrew which he has and Maximus retained: 'Lest I become as one thrown aside, wandering after the flock of your companions (Ne fiam quasi decepta, vagabunda, errans, by occasion of the flock of others).' And the Hebrew word is also thus explained; and not only 'covered, clothed,' a signification not well suited to this place. I have spoken well enough of this from Psellus and others. The subject is the Bride, so anxious to find her Bridegroom's flock and afraid of being deceived in it by likeness to others: 'parabalei' (Hesychius: 'apatēseis, you will deceive'); and he gives this as the first and well-known, common signification of the word. Suidas also: 'parablēdēn: deceitfully, fallaciously.' And nothing of it occurs in it from Thucydides, which the author of the Thesaurus tries to downplay.

Esra vult א esse formativum, quasi a [Hebrew word, not transcribed] ex eo quod stillæ ejusmodi rotundæ sint ac quasi convolutæ. Sic et βόλοι δρόσου, quod quasi globuli jaciantur, voce satis ingeniose excogitata τοῖς LXX. At quod Xyst. habent βῶλοι, glebæ roris, nullaque varia lectione interpr. affert, nullus probo; nec video quænam apta metaphora, ut roris stillæ, quod optime reddidit Vulg., dicantur glebæ. Quod etiam massa redditur ea vox, βῶλος σιδήρου Eccli. xxii, et βῶλος χρυσέα, pro sole, Apoll. Rhodii schol. ex Euripide, nihil congruit, quod massa, magni aliquid ponderis sit, non exile quid, uti stillæ roris: quarum stillare, spargi est et jaci, τὸ βάλλεσθαι. Sic etiam Vatabl. aliique interpretes. Codex Alex. συνοχὰς καὶ βώλους; in quem nihil hic necesse inquirere.
unplaced.anchorLine: σιʹ. Βόλοι μὲν δρόσου (g), γῆς μεθύσκουσιν αὔλα-
unplaced.en: 'Drops (bolo) of dew.' So the old lexica cite it from Gregory too, and the Greek Bibles have 'drops of dew'; and so even the Hebrew [Hebrew word], in which word Aben Ezra would have the aleph be formative, as though from [Hebrew word], because such drops are round and as it were rolled together. So also 'bolo of dew,' as if little globes were thrown, a word quite ingeniously devised by the Seventy. But as for the Sixtine translators' having 'bolo,' clods of dew, and offering no variant reading, I do not approve; nor do I see what apt metaphor there is by which drops of dew would be called clods. That this word is also rendered 'mass' (bolos of iron in Ecclesiasticus xxii, and bolos of gold for the sun in the scholiast on Apollonius of Rhodes, from Euripides) is no support, since a mass is something of great weight, not something slight, like drops of dew, of which to drip, to be scattered, is to be cast, the verb ballesthai. So also Vatablus and other interpreters. The Alexandrian codex has 'sunochas kai bolous'; into which there is no need to inquire here.

unplaced.text: Καὶ τῆς γείτονος μονάδος. Videtur voce μονάδος significare, qua Deus unus ipse et singularis cognoscitur, nulla personarum distinctione; quam excedere necesse est, altiori cognitione, ut Deitatem in Trinitate intelligamus; et non solum δυάδα, binarium, qua voce Greg. Orat. in diem Natal. exque illo Maximus, creaturam intelligunt; quæ præsertim constant ex materia et forma. Vicinam dicit hanc μονάδα, quod proclive sit et innatum, ut sic Deum intelligamus. Est enim hæc inter ea quæ Paulus vocat nota Dei.
unplaced.anchorLine: καὶ τῆς γείτονος μονάδος (h) ἄνωθεν μὴ ὀφθεὶς·
unplaced.en: 'And of the neighboring monad.' He seems to mean by the word 'monad' that by which God is known as one and singular, without any distinction of persons; which must be transcended by a higher knowledge, so that we understand the Godhead in the Trinity; and not only the 'dyad', the 'binary', by which word Gregory in the Oration on the Nativity, and Maximus after him, understand the creature, which consists especially of matter and form. He calls this monad 'neighboring' because it is ready to hand and innate, that we may thus understand God. For it is among the things that Paul calls 'the known of God.'

unplaced.text: Εἴσω τῶν ὁρωμένων. Id ita dictum Maximo videatur, quod mens ipsas eorum rationes in eis contempletur; et in illis τὰ ἀσώματα (res scilicet spiritales ac intelligibilia) cognoscat: ex quibus assurgit ad ipsum ὑπερούσιον Λόγον (Deum nimirum) quantum ex rebus a nobis cognosci potest. Sic cap. 589 et 590, ubi etiam necessario exigit, τὸ ἔξω γενέσθαι τῆς προσπαθείας τῶν αἰσθητῶν· ab omni terrenorum affectu excedere ac libidine, quo mentis illa puritas, de qua hic sermo est præstatur. Verum expeditius sit, scripsisse Maximum ἔξω τῶν ὁρωμένων· qua enim mente sic visibilibus excedimus, contemplando divina, terrena omnia, ac quidquid in illis dignum æmulatione videtur περιμάχητον, omnino contemnimus.
unplaced.anchorLine: ὁρωμένων (i) παραπέμποντες, τοσούτου πίμπλανται
unplaced.en: 'Within the things seen.' Maximus seems to have said this because the mind contemplates the very reasons of the things in them and knows in them the incorporeal things (that is, spiritual and intelligible realities), from which it rises to the supersubstantial Word himself (God, that is), as far as he can be known by us from things. So in chapters 589 and 590, where he likewise requires of necessity 'to be outside the sympathy of sensible things': to depart from all affection for earthly things and from lust, by which that purity of mind of which he speaks is secured. But it would be easier to say that Maximus wrote 'outside the things seen' (exo ton horomenon): for by that mind with which we thus pass beyond visible things in contemplating divine things, we altogether despise all earthly things and whatever in them seems worth contending for (perimachēton).

unplaced.text: Ὁ φιλοκάλῳ πάθει. Quod φιλοκάλῳ τὸ φιλότιμον jungit Maximus, argumento est, sic in partem vitii illud usurpare, ut superfluum duntaxat cultum elegantiamque significet, cujus amor etiam iis qui ad pietatem exercent, obstaculo esse solet sublimioris volatus in oratione; quomodo ab Hesychio τὸ, φιλόκαλος, φιλόκοσμος exponitur: cum alioqui ea vox communius sonet in bonum, ac pro honesti studioso accipiatur: quandoque etiam dicatur de amore corporum. Sic φιλοκαλία Socrati objecta, ac si dictum fuisset παιδεραστία. Greg. de pavone perinde ambo hæc conjunxit φιλόκαλον καὶ φιλότιμον· ad notandum animal pulchritudinis amans, eaque sibi placens ac ambitiosum; ex quo Maximus transferre potuit in mores hominum.
unplaced.anchorLine: ολάλῳ πάθει (j) καὶ φιλοτίμῳ κρατούμενος.
unplaced.en: 'By a love-of-beauty passion.' That Maximus joins 'ambition' (philotimon) to 'love of the beautiful' (philokalo) is evidence that he takes the term in the sense of a vice, so that it denotes only superfluous adornment and elegance, the love of which is wont to be an obstacle even to those who practise piety, to a more sublime flight in prayer; as Hesychius explains 'philokalos' by 'philokosmos' (world-loving): though otherwise the word more commonly sounds in a good sense and is taken for one devoted to what is honorable; at times it is even said of the love of bodies. So 'philokalia' was charged against Socrates, as if it were said 'pederasty.' Gregory, concerning the peacock, likewise joined both: 'philokalon and philotimon', to mark an animal fond of beauty, pleased with itself and ambitious; from which Maximus could transfer it to the characters of men.

unplaced.text: Διὰ τοῦ ἀποστερήματος. Sensus videtur, sic colendam pacem cum proximo, ut ejus causa omnem in eum patientiam exhibeamus, cujus ipsi nobis in Christo rei sumus; summam scilicet, ut quasi fraudatio Christianæ in nobis patientiæ sit, seu ex illa subtractio, quod sic in illum patientes simus. Sicut et fraudatio victus viduæ fuit, quod duo minuta ad necessarium usum reposita, sic in gazophylacium miserit; non superflua mittens, uti divites, sed ἐκ τοῦ ὑστερήματος αὐτῆς πάντα, quidquid in summa illa egestate illi suppetebat.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἱς εἰρήνης, διὰ τοῦ ἀποστερήματος (k) τῆς ἐν Κυ-
unplaced.en: 'Through the deprivation.' The sense seems to be that peace with one's neighbor is to be cultivated so that for his sake we show him all patience, of which we are ourselves guilty in Christ; the sum of it being that there should be, as it were, a defrauding of Christian patience in us, or a subtraction from it, in that we are thus patient toward him. As also the defrauding of the widow's livelihood was that she cast into the treasury two mites laid aside for necessary use; not sending in what was superfluous, like the rich, but 'out of her want' everything, whatever in that utmost poverty she had to support her.

unplaced.text: Φαντασίαις οὐ σαλεύονται. Negatio omnino incommoda ac expungenda. Est enim caput istud, superioris quasi scholium; qua sæpius methodo Maximus utitur. Ei igitur qui prope ad ἀπάθειαν accedit, sed eam necdum perfecte adeptus est, id tribuit quod in vitiis minimum est; nudam scilicet cogitationem seu rei informationem; sicque deinceps reliqua reliquis; ad usque tactum, qui in sensibus crassior est, ac proinde summam denotat in rerum abusu exercitam libidinem; exstincta quasi arguente conscientia luceque rationis absorpta pro libidinis abundantia ac victoria: quod est sic ἀλύπως, nullo doloris sensu, in eo versari. Sic cap. 70, ἐμπάθειαν σώματος esse ait, et de illa tactum prædicari, ἁφήν· qui sensus maxime corporeus: ἡδυπάθεια vero, animæ; de qua prædicentur αἱ λοιπαὶ αἰσθήσεις, sensus reliqui; paulo scilicet spiritaliores; quorum minor vis quam ut omnino subjiciant animum, aut ejus omnem dolorem ex contrarii pugna auferant. Hos ait animo voluptarios σχέσεσι, affectibus commoveri; cap. vero 72, pati quidem illos interius ait, seu affici, sic tamen ut peccati vim (ἐνέργειαν) imbecilliorem ratione habeant. Sint fere ἡδυπαθεῖς, in quorum persona Paulus tanta de se loquitur Rom. vii, in quibus pugna illa legis mentis, ejusque, quæ in membris exsistit, id est concupiscentiæ: quam plerique non sentiunt, non quod ἀπαθεῖς, plene jam affectuum victores in tranquillitatis arce sint constituti; sed quod potius stupore ἐμπαθεῖς, sic illis mancipati, ut nec quod mancipati sunt, vero ullo animi sensu intelligant.
unplaced.anchorLine: [οὐ] σαλεύονται (l)· ἐπιθυμίαις δὲ, οἱ μετριοπα-
unplaced.en: 'They are not shaken by phantasies.' The negation is wholly awkward and ought to be deleted. For this chapter is, as it were, a scholion on the preceding one, by a method Maximus often uses. So to him who comes close to apatheia but has not yet perfectly attained it, he attributes what is least in vices: bare thought, or the forming of the thing in the mind; and so on in turn with the rest, up to touch, which is the coarser of the senses and therefore marks the highest degree of libido exercised in the abuse of things; it is quenched, as though conscience accused and the light of reason were swallowed up, by the abundance and victory of libido: that is, to be in it 'painlessly,' with no sense of pain. So in chapter 70 he says that the passion of the body is empathia, and that touch is predicated of it (haphe), the most corporeal sense; but hedypatheia (soft indulgence) belongs to the soul, of which the remaining senses are predicated, somewhat more spiritual, whose force is too small to subject the mind entirely or take away all its pain from the contrary struggle. These he says are moved in mind as voluptuaries by 'attachments' (schesesi), by affections; but in chapter 72 he says they suffer inwardly, that is are affected, yet so that they have the force (energeia) of sin weaker than reason. These would be roughly the hedypatheis, in whose person Paul says so much of himself in Rom. vii, in whom there is that struggle of the law of the mind and of that which exists in the members, that is, of concupiscence: which most do not feel, not because they are apathetic, already full victors set in the citadel of tranquillity, but rather because by stupor they are empatheis, so enslaved to them that they do not understand with any true sense of the mind that they are enslaved.

unplaced.text: Εἰς τὸν τῆς μετριοπαθείας λιμένα. Non satis cohærere videtur, quod hic μετριοπάθειαν portum dicit, cum superius, c. 228, medios posuerit quos μετριοπαθεῖς vocat, eorum quos accedere ait ad ἀπάθειαν, et quos vocat ἡδυπαθεῖς· qui et jactentur ἐπιθυμίαις, cupiditatibus, desideriis. Portus enim, in quo tuta sit ac tranquilla statio, ἀπαθείας magis videatur, in qua non sit ullis jactari fluctibus, σαλεύεσθαι, sed pace frui ac quiescere. Nisi forte hoc vult Maximus, omnem nostram hic ἀπάθειαν, temperationem quamdam esse affectuum et μετριοπάθειαν· quorum motus nec perfectis desint, illisque jactari, cum tamen se illis abduci minime sinant, sintque velut navis ipsa in anchora σαλευομένη, tum etiam cum portum videtur tenere: ut nec tunc omne absit periculum, sed semper vigilare necesse sit, esseque cura sollicitum.
unplaced.anchorLine: δύναται λιμένα (m) εἰσέρχεσθαι, ὁ βίᾳ τὰς
unplaced.en: 'Into the harbor of moderation of passion.' It seems not quite consistent that he here calls metriopatheia a harbor, when above, chapter 228, he placed in the middle those whom he calls metriopatheis, of those whom he says approach to [continues on the next page]. apatheia, and whom he calls hedypatheis, who are also tossed by desires (epithymiai), cupidities. For a harbor, in which the station is safe and tranquil, would seem rather to belong to apatheia, in which one is not tossed (saleuesthai) by any waves but enjoys peace and rest. Unless perhaps Maximus means this: that our whole apatheia here is a certain tempering of the affections, and moderation of passion (metriopatheia); whose motions are not wanting even in the perfect, and they are tossed by them, though they by no means allow themselves to be carried away by them, and are like a ship itself riding at anchor (saleuomene), even when it seems to hold the harbor: so that not even then is all danger absent, but it is always necessary to be watchful, and to be anxious in care.

unplaced.en: 'But they pair off.' I have added the particle 'de' and in what follows changed to 'kai': 'hoi de hedeos; hoi kai hedeos', because the whole structure of the passage plainly requires it, and so everything is smooth and clear: for these are two clauses following by a fuller explanation. Furthermore this is most salutary teaching: beginnings are to be earnestly guarded against; evil grows little by little and at last becomes insuperable; and the example is well known: 'the solitary wild beast' (monios agrios), 'a singular wild one,' that is, a boar, which is also called by us 'sanglier': a wild and solitary pig; which you may restrain for a time in its tender age; but once grown, you cannot, by any industry, restrain it from tearing down the vineyard into which you have admitted it. That in Psalm lxxix, 14, the same animal is signified in both halves of the verse, and that the 'monion agrion' is the 'sus ek drymou' (boar out of the wood), Bochart tries to show at length in book iii, chapter 29, vol. i of his History of the Animals of Sacred Scripture. So the Seventy certainly understood it in rendering it thus, although Cyril has 'wild ass' (onon agrion), as Hesychius too advised, and the Arabic rendered it in the same manner, and the Polyglot has it. Others more commonly render 'beast of the desert,' as Symmachus also, so that it is rather a generic noun, the Hebrew [ziz], signifying 'beast' rather than a certain species. The Chaldee: 'wild cock.' R. David: 'wild beast'; R. Solomon: 'reptile'; Aben Ezra: 'birds, fowl.' Quite differently the Seventy in Psalm xlix, 11, 'beauty of the field' (horaiotes agrou), 'species agri', although the Hebrew words are the same, and the whole sequence demands to be explained of beasts in general or of wild animals. To say 'form or ornament of the field, or of the desert' would seem very remote and plainly enigmatic. The scholion from Symmachus at that Psalm lxxix, 'creatures of the wilderness,' is not well referred in the Sixtine edition to the words 'sus ek drymou,' by which a definite species of animal is denoted, in Greek as in Hebrew, one very well known; but to the following 'monios agrios,' to which corresponds in the Hebrew that word of such wide signification, which could signify any animal; and which is the same as the Greek 'knodalon' (beast).

unplaced.en: 'Being perfect.' There was a foul error in the copy: 'ateleis' (imperfect) — I do not know whether also in the autograph. It is clear at any rate that this was unfitting, and that I did not rashly indulge myself in changing it, and by the change restoring Maximus to Maximus. The talk is plainly of those who, since they seem to themselves to have already seized the citadel of virtue and to be perfect, think they must indulge their genius, as though they no longer needed stricter discipline: which not only the unwary spiritual draw to the relaxation of the body, in matters that can be indifferent, but even profane heretics to base and unspeakable lusts; against which Maximus guards superbly, ending his golden and truly ascetic chapters, which strengthen to all virtue from the rule of Christ, with so holy a colophon.
